title: Still Operational
revision: Draft 3.8 — developmental edit and mission stakes
paragraphs: The first sound Andrew Walker heard that morning was singing.
It came from the kitchen at six fourteen, loud enough to carry down the corridor. Darius had a good voice when he wanted one. This morning he appeared to be inventing a song as he went.

From the other bed, Nicolas Vallée dragged a pillow over his face. Nico's oversized sleep shirt hung loosely from narrow shoulders, making him look even smaller than his five-foot-six frame. A riot of dark brown curls poked over the pillow.
“Does he know it's six in the morning?” Nico asked.
“He's making breakfast,” Andrew mumbled.
“He can make breakfast quietly.”
From the kitchen came another enthusiastic verse, followed by a loud metallic crash.
The singing stopped.
“Sorry!” Darius called from down the hall.
Nico lifted the edge of his pillow. “Was that an apology to us or the pot?”
“Knowing Darius? Both.”
“Good. Tell him the pot accepts. I don't.”
Andrew laughed despite himself.
A moment later, Darius started singing again.
Nico stared at the ceiling. “Unbelievable.”

Nico lowered the pillow enough for Andrew to catch his hazel eyes, a scattering of freckles across his cheeks and small straight nose, and the familiar crooked grin. One side of his curls had been flattened against the mattress while the other stuck out wildly. Still grinning, he began tapping a rhythm against the metal bedframe with his fingertips.
“Now you're doing it,” Andrew said.
“That's different,” Nico said. “I'm keeping time.”
“For what?”
“The song I'll write about being denied sleep by the military.”
“Catchy title.”
“I'll shorten it for the album.”
Andrew reached for the clock above his pillow. It still read 06:14. He had been awake less than a minute and had already lost an argument he wasn't sure he'd joined.

Their sleeping room had once been a records office in a municipal maintenance depot. Two narrow bunks filled most of it; an old noticeboard had left a clean rectangle on the wall. A radiator made an occasional hopeful click without producing any heat. Andrew's uniform hung from a hook beside the door. On the shelf above his bed sat a torch, two secondhand novels, and a wristwatch he'd been meaning to repair.

Andrew swung his legs over the edge of the bunk. He was nineteen, lean and wiry rather than imposing, and his feet searched for the socks he'd left beside the bed. Running a military outpost was not among the things he'd imagined doing at his age.

The orders on his desk still read Unteroffizier Andrew Walker, acting commander. Matthias Adler, the Feldwebel who had once led all twelve of them, was gone. Andrew had been his second-in-command, and the appointment had brought him the responsibilities without the comfort of a higher rank.
He pulled on his socks before his feet touched the cold floor. Across the room Nico had gone back to composing his song, this time without words.
Three knocks sounded at the door.
“Andrew?” Darius called. “Are you up?”
“Not by choice,” Andrew answered.
“Can you try something before breakfast?” Darius asked.
Nico pulled the pillow over his face again. “Whatever he wants you to try, say it tastes brilliant. Then he'll go away.”
Andrew opened the door.

Darius Okafor stood in the corridor wearing a flour-dusted apron stretched over his broad chest. At nineteen he was already six foot three, the tallest and broadest of the squad, with powerful shoulders that made the narrow doorway look poorly designed. He had deep brown skin, short, tightly curled black hair trimmed close at the sides, a broad nose, and gentle brown eyes set in a face that seemed perpetually on the verge of a shy smile. Flour coated his large hands, which were more often marked by garden soil or small cooking burns than by anything from the range. In one hand he carried a spoon; in the other, a little bowl of porridge that looked almost comically small against his fingers. Warm cinnamon drifted toward Andrew.
“I added the last of the apples,” Darius said. “Tell me whether it's too sweet.”
Andrew accepted a spoonful. The porridge was thick and hot, with pieces of apple that still held their shape. He swallowed, then took a second taste before returning the spoon.
“Don't change anything,” Andrew said.
Darius's face eased into a smile. “Not even more cinnamon?”
“If you have more cinnamon, hide it before Nico finds out.”
“I'm awake,” Nico called from the room. “And I can hear you insulting me.”
“Then get dressed,” Darius called back. “Breakfast at seven.”

Andrew watched him hurry toward the kitchen, humming again. Darius was the unit's designated supply hand as well as its self-appointed cook, and he took both jobs seriously. Last week he'd bartered two loaves of bread for a driver's bruised apples; she'd wanted something fresh for her children, and the flour he'd given up wasn't easily replaced. He'd turned what might have been a snack into breakfast for eight.
Andrew shut the door.
Nico lowered his pillow once more. “So? Was it actually good?”
“Unfortunately.”
“Why unfortunately?”
“Now we have to help with the dishes.”
Nico sat up. “That's extortion.”
“Tell him that when you ask for seconds.”

In the washroom Andrew faced a spotted mirror and tried to flatten his thick, dark waves. Someone in the unit had cut them unevenly around his ears, and the result looked no better this morning. His warm olive-toned face, straight nose, defined jaw, and brown eyes under expressive dark brows looked younger than the stubble he kept forgetting to shave. He gave up, pulled on his uniform and stepped into the waking outpost. Pipes ticked in the walls. A radio was on in the common room. Through a rain-streaked window he could see the hangar across the courtyard, its doors framed by concrete barriers and cable runs. The machines inside were among the reasons people could still live behind this part of the defensive perimeter.

The depot stood in Germany, inside the last territory humanity had managed to keep from the Reclaimed. Elsewhere the defenses had fallen; survivors had made their way here from countries that no longer had a safe place to offer them. The enemy was no rumor or mysterious name. Andrew had seen the human tissue joined to machinery, and the way a mass of those things could move together as if receiving one thought. He would be perfectly happy not to see them before breakfast.

The broadcast mentioned another eastern road closure, a civilian supply convoy held overnight after the relay went silent, and new restrictions on fuel and cooking oil. The announcer gave the hours when people could exchange ration slips for water. Nobody at the depot stopped to listen to these bulletins anymore, though everybody heard them.

On his way past the noticeboard, Andrew noticed a fresh handwritten offer pinned beneath the duty schedule: NEED WINTER BOOTS, SIZE 43. CAN REPAIR TWO HEATERS OR TRADE SOAP. There were three more notes beside it, each listing what someone needed and what they had to offer. Nobody had written a price.
In the common room, Akari Sato was taking a photograph of an empty chair.

Akari rose from her crouch and stepped sideways to adjust the camera before taking another picture. She was petite, barely five foot four, with a slender, athletic build and so much restless energy that standing still seemed to be an effort. Her long, straight black hair was pulled into a high ponytail, already slipping loose at the neck, with wisps framing an oval face and a small, delicate nose. Dark brown eyes followed every change in the light, and her bright smile suggested she'd already thought of something amusing. A faded sweatshirt hung off one shoulder, one sleeve pushed above the elbow; dark trousers and a worn camera strap completed an outfit she'd clearly assembled for comfort rather than inspection. Akari was the unit's reconnaissance specialist, which explained her eye for detail, if not her fascination with chairs.
Andrew stopped. “Should I ask what that chair did?”
“I'm testing the light,” Akari said.
“It seems to be behaving.”
“Unlike my usual subjects.”

A paperback lay on the nearby table. Sera Bell sat beside it, sorting Akari's photographs into two careful piles. Slender and a little under five foot six, she had medium-brown skin, a softly rounded nose, and full lips that pressed together whenever a picture failed her inspection. Long, dark curls were gathered into a loose bun, though a few escaped beside her cheeks. Amber-brown eyes, almost golden where the morning light caught them, moved from one photograph to the next with the same careful attention she gave the XR-17s' electronic diagnostics. An oversized dark sweater swallowed her narrow shoulders, its sleeves pulled halfway over her hands. She seemed content to let Akari supply the conversation.
“You asked me to help choose the best pictures,” Sera said to Akari, “then you went to photograph furniture.”
“The chair won't move while I test the exposure.”
“It doesn't need to. The photographs from last month are still out of focus,” Sera replied.
Akari turned to Andrew. “See? This is what I get for asking for help.”
“Sera's right,” Andrew said.
“Traitor,” Akari muttered.
Sera set one photograph on the smaller pile. “That's the good one.”
Akari leaned over to inspect it. Their shoulders touched, and for a moment she forgot whatever complaint she'd intended to make.
Andrew reached for the coffee tin. It was empty.
“That's disappointing,” he said.
Akari swung the camera toward him. “Hold still. Your face is excellent.”
“Don't you dare.”
She took the photograph.
“Akari.”
“I'm calling it Man Learns There Is No Coffee.”
“Gallery opening at noon?” Andrew asked.
“Only if you attend,” Akari said.

The common-room door opened before Andrew could invent an appropriate punishment. Mara Venn came in carrying a waterproof map case beneath one arm. His appointed deputy handled patrol planning with a precision Andrew had learned to trust, though her formal rank was only Hauptgefreiter. At five foot eight she had a compact, athletic build, strong shoulders, and upright posture. Her long, dark chestnut hair was tied into a practical ponytail, with damp strands escaping around an angular face, high cheekbones, and a straight nose. Gray-green eyes swept over the room before settling on Andrew; the familiar line between her brows suggested she'd already found something that needed fixing. Her uniform was neat above the waist, though rain had darkened the fabric and mud marked her trouser cuffs and worn boots. She put a small packet beside the empty coffee tin.
“From the north watch,” she said. “They owed me a favor.”

Andrew inspected the packet. Real coffee, sealed and dry. Nobody had seen it in a regular supply allocation for months. He turned it over as if it might turn out to be a trick. “You are my favorite person.”
“You said that to Darius yesterday,” Mara reminded him.
“Darius made bread yesterday.”
Mara pulled out a chair. “I'll forgive you when you've read the route changes.”
Andrew filled the kettle and set it on the heater. “What changes?”
“The eastern crossing is nearly underwater. Tomorrow's patrol needs a different approach.”

The relay station beyond the eastern works handled radio traffic between observation posts and the escorts bringing civilians and supplies toward the defended towns. It had been cutting out for days. A convoy had spent last night at a roadblock rather than enter the blind stretch, and the next supply run was due tomorrow evening. Andrew's unit had orders to secure a route for the technicians tomorrow morning and keep the road covered while they repaired the link.
Andrew had planned the most direct approach. Mara had spent the morning discovering why it might be a mistake.
“Let me get coffee,” he said, “and we'll spread the map out.”
“Good,” Mara said. “I'd hate to argue with you before you're capable of reasoning.”
“That's very thoughtful.”
Akari raised her camera. “I want all eight of us outside at four. Group photograph.”
Mara didn't turn around. “Why?”
“Because we don't have a new one. The last group shot was ages ago, and I'm putting a current one on the kitchen wall.”
“It's raining,” Andrew said.
“Then I'll have excellent reflections on the concrete.”
“Akari,” Sera said, “you're not taking your camera into the rain.”
“I know. I said if the rain stops.”
“You didn't.”
“Then I meant to,” Akari said.
Sera handed Akari the photograph she'd selected. Akari smiled at it, slipped it into a protective sleeve, and looked back at the others.
“Four o'clock,” she repeated. “Attendance mandatory.”
“Do I get a vote?” Andrew asked.
“You can vote on where to stand,” Akari answered.
Mara unrolled the map. Andrew sat opposite her as the kettle began to hiss, grateful to have something useful to argue about.
From the kitchen came Darius's singing again. This time, Nico joined in from the corridor, deliberately half a beat behind.
By seven, Darius had filled the common room with the smell of toasted bread and apples.

He set the porridge in the middle of the table so that everyone could help themselves. There was enough for eight, provided Nico didn't start treating the serving spoon like a personal challenge. Darius stood beside the pot until Mara had taken a bowl and Yelena had arrived from the morning watch.
Andrew held up his own bowl. “You were right about the cinnamon.”
Darius raised an eyebrow. “More?”
“Just enough.”
“Thank you.” Darius tried to sound dignified, then smiled.
Nico took his first mouthful and stopped talking.
For a moment the only sounds were the spoon against his bowl and rain at the window.
“That good?” Darius asked.
Nico swallowed. “I was checking for an unreasonable advantage.”
“In porridge?” Mara asked.
“Darius has clearly been practicing while we're asleep,” Nico said.
“I've been cooking for you for months,” Darius said.
“That's what makes it suspicious,” Nico insisted.

Sera, sitting beside Akari, slid the remaining apple pieces toward Nico without looking up from a small puzzle book. Nico accepted them with a quiet thanks. Andrew noticed the gesture; Sera often gave things away when nobody was paying attention.

After breakfast Mara spread the map across the cleared table. The others drifted toward their assignments, leaving Andrew and Mara with two mugs of coffee and a pencil that had been sharpened down to a stub.
Mara touched the eastern crossing. “The approach is flooded. Yesterday the road markers were still visible. This morning I could barely make out the top of the nearest one.”
“Can an XR-17 get through?” Andrew asked.
“Probably, if the shoulder holds. That doesn't help if one of us breaks down. We'd have no room to turn with a tow cable.”

Andrew pictured the crossing: a narrow bridge, soft ground beside the road, and fields that lay open on either side. The direct route had one advantage. It kept the squad close to the observation posts for most of the trip, which meant fewer places for the Reclaimed to approach unseen.
He could have argued for it. Part of him wanted to. He'd drawn that route himself.
Mara laid a second pencil line across the south edge of the map.

“The service road adds two kilometers,” she said. “But there's hard ground beyond the culvert and a paved lot near the old workshops. We can bring a damaged machine through without blocking the others.”
“What happens to our sightline at the culvert?”
“Poor for about three hundred meters,” Mara said. “We can have two machines hold the approaches while the technicians' vehicle goes through.”
Andrew studied the small square she'd marked at the far end of the road.
“That's also where the convoy escorts check in,” he said.
Mara nodded. “If the relay fails again, the next convoy waits too. The clinic shipment is on that run, and nobody wants to explain another day's delay.”

The direct route was shorter. He still didn't like the extra blind stretch. But Mara had a clear recovery plan, and she'd gone out in the rain to check the surface instead of trusting the markings on the map.
“Let's use the service road,” Andrew said. “Put the hardstand on the withdrawal sheet. Ask Yelena whether the west watch can cover the culvert during our crossing.”
Mara looked at him. “You're not going to argue about the bridge?”
“Would it improve the bridge?”
“Probably not.”
“Then save us both the effort.”
She took the pencil. “You're getting easier to work with.”
“I'll try not to make it a habit.”

Mara went back to the map. Andrew watched her mark the revised route, then added his initials beside the change. There was a time when he'd have taken a different plan as a challenge to his judgment. He remembered that version of himself with no particular affection.
“Thanks for checking it,” he said.
Mara's pencil stopped. “That's the job.”
“Still. Thanks.”
She gave him a quick nod and continued drawing.
At nine, the hangar doors opened just wide enough to admit the gray morning light.

Their eight XR-17s occupied a double row of maintenance bays. Each machine crouched on six articulated legs, its compact armored body hanging low between them. Scuffed plates concealed most of the internal structure, leaving the dark joints, pistons, and bundled cables exposed where the limbs needed to move. A heavy cannon sat above the cockpit on a rotating turret, flanked by matching vertical missile pods. Below the armored canopy, a smaller rotary cannon projected from the machine's nose. A circular reactor housing bulged from the rear.
The machines had been manufactured to defend Germany when the rest of the world could no longer keep a defensive line intact. Their technology was impressive. Their maintenance records were less so.

One of Andrew's machines had a mismatched foot. Another carried a panel salvaged from a destroyed vehicle. Replacement components still appeared on requisition forms, but increasingly the only way to get one was to strip it from something beyond repair. Every cockpit had its own collection of improvised fixes, nicknames, and tiny personal decorations that weren't in the manuals.
Juno Kade, the unit's lead mechanic as well as an XR-17 pilot, was under the left-front leg of his machine.

A few uneven tufts of vivid golden-blond hair stuck out beneath the orange-lensed goggles pushed up on Juno's head. Black headphones with orange detailing rested against the raised yellow collar of his dark mechanic's jacket, whose pockets were stained with grease and crowded with tools. A narrow strip of cyan trim ran along one shoulder. From where Andrew stood, only Juno's boots, one elbow, and part of his lean frame were visible beyond the machine's front armor.
“Morning,” Andrew called.
A metal tool clinked against the floor.
“Depends what kind of morning you mean,” Juno answered.
“Is the bearing coming out?”
“Yes.”
“Are you coming out?”
“Eventually.”
Nico, the unit's radio technician when he wasn't piloting his own XR-17, knelt beside a tray of parts and lifted his hand. “I could pull him out.”
“Do not pull me out,” Juno said.
A harsh scrape cut across the hangar. The tool Juno had been forcing against the stubborn collar slipped, striking the stand with a crack. Nico lurched backward, nearly upsetting the parts tray.
“Juno!” Nico shouted. “I told you to wait for the proper tool!”
Andrew crossed the space between them. “Out from under there. Now.”

Juno slid clear on the trolley, still clutching the improvised lever. At roughly five foot seven, he was slight and wiry, with narrow shoulders and grease-smeared forearms that never seemed to stop moving. Bright blue eyes stood out against the smudge across his cheek; a slightly pointed nose and narrow chin gave his youthful face an almost permanently mischievous look. Usually that look came with a grin. Right now he was more annoyed than frightened. “I almost had it. That collar was moving.”
“The tool was moving,” Nico said. His smile had vanished. “Toward your face.”
Juno gave the bar a guilty glance. “It would've been fine.”

“You don't know that,” Andrew said. He kept his voice level, which was harder than raising it. “You know how much force is sitting in that joint. Don't gamble your hands because you don't feel like walking to stores.”
Juno's jaw tightened. For a second Andrew thought he would argue. Then Juno set the bar on the bench. “Fine. I'll get the extractor.”
“And Nico checks the setup with you before you start again,” Andrew added.
“I can do that,” Nico said. He was still watching the place the tool had struck.

When Juno returned with the proper extractor, Nico double-checked the supports against the checklist he'd been keeping. Juno freed the collar without another incident, rolled out on the trolley, and wiped grease from one wrist.
“The left-front bearing catches under load,” he explained. “You can feel it in the seat when you turn. The retaining collar's coming off, but it doesn't want to surrender gracefully.”
“How long?” Andrew asked.

“I'll fit the replacement by lunch,” Juno said. “Then I want a walking test, a loaded turn, and a controlled cannon shot on the range. The recoil will put a different kind of stress through that joint. If the bearing's still binding, I'd rather find out here than tomorrow.”
Andrew nodded. “All three, plus a look at the bearing housing afterward. We're not clearing the machine just because it can walk in a straight line.”
“Agreed,” Juno said.
Juno agreed readily when the stakes involved his machine. Andrew wished getting him to extend that same caution to his own body were as easy.
“What about the old bearing?” Nico asked.
“Scrap for the leg,” Juno said. “But there's good steel in the outer race. I can probably use part of it for the workshop's rotating fixture once I've cleaned it.”
Andrew looked at the scarred metal ring on the bench. “Don't put it anywhere near a flight assembly.”
“I'm not that stupid,” Juno said.

In the next bay, Sera Bell sat on a crate with a diagnostic screen balanced across her knees. She had been following the readings throughout the repair, far less interested in the noise around her than the small errors appearing on the display.
“Juno,” Sera said, “you have a second fault.”
Juno turned. “You told me the bearing was the fault.”
“I told you it was a fault,” Sera said.
She angled the screen toward Andrew. Red spikes interrupted the smooth load graph every few seconds.
“Loose vibration pickup,” Sera explained. “The software thinks the left side has detached. The actual temperature and load readings look sensible. Those spikes don't.”
Andrew looked at the raised leg. “It hasn't detached, right?”
Sera regarded him.
“No,” she said. “I would have led with that.”
Juno grinned at her. “You really know how to reassure people.”
“It's a skill.”
As she unplugged the diagnostic lead, a folded page from the puzzle book she'd brought to breakfast slipped out from behind her tablet. She retrieved it before Nico could see the solution.
“Is that the answer?” Nico asked.
“Yes,” Sera said, sliding it into her pocket. “You'll have to solve it yourself.”

Andrew let the conversation settle while he checked the repaired setup. The supports were locked properly now, and the assembly was marked for alignment. Juno knew the machine better than anyone in the room. That was precisely why Andrew expected better judgment from him.
“I'll leave you to it,” Andrew told Juno. “Mara can arrange the firing lane. And from here on, no improvised shortcuts. The test doesn't begin until the repair is signed off.”
Juno looked up. “You aren't staying to supervise?”
“No,” Andrew said. “I'm trusting you to follow the procedure. There's a difference.”
For a brief instant, Juno's expression lost its usual grin.
Then Juno glanced toward Nico, who was still checking the workbench, and picked up his wrench. “All right. No more heroics with the bearing.”
“You'll survive.”
Nico held out the clipboard. “Can I write that down as an official statement?”
“Only if you spell it correctly,” Andrew said.
He left them with Sera's diagnostic screen glowing beside the raised leg. Outside, the rain had thinned to a fine mist.
The north watch post overlooked a broad strip of land that might once have been pleasant countryside.

There were fields, a half-collapsed warehouse, and a road that ran toward the interior settlements. Beyond them sat a line of earthworks and concrete defenses. Farther east, the outposts became fewer, and Andrew tried not to think too long about what happened beyond the line on bad days.

Yelena Sokolova leaned against the watch post's railing with a dented metal mug cupped between her hands. She was around five foot seven, slender but sturdily built, with long limbs and a relaxed posture Andrew knew not to mistake for inattention. Cold had reddened her fair cheeks and straight nose. Her strong cheekbones and defined jaw made the raised eyebrow she gave him particularly effective, while pale gray eyes regarded him with their usual tired, unimpressed look. Her long ash-brown hair was braided thickly and tucked inside her military jacket, though the wind had pulled loose strands across her face. A bandage packet stuck out of an overfull pocket. She was their combat medic, but the shortage of hands meant she still drew regular watch shifts.
“You're early,” she said as Andrew climbed the stairs.
“I'm exactly on time.”
“Then the clock's wrong.”
Andrew took the binoculars from the case. “Any movement?”
“Two patrol vehicles, one flatbed heading west, and a cat.”
“A cat?”
“Very suspicious,” Yelena said. “Four legs, bad attitude. Probably an infiltrator.”
Yelena pointed toward a narrow gap behind the storehouse. A small gray cat sat beneath the overhang, watching the rain.
Andrew lowered the binoculars. “You put water down for it.”
“Did I?”
“There's a dish beside it.”
“Perhaps somebody else values civilized behavior.”
“You're on the morning watch. Who else has been up here?”
Yelena sipped her tea instead of answering.
Beside her lay a paperback with two people standing on the cover in clothes far too clean for anyone Andrew knew. He turned it around to read the title.
“Is this the terrible book you were complaining about yesterday?”
“It's much worse today,” Yelena said.
“You're nearly finished.”
“I want to know how bad it gets.”
Andrew read the summary on the back. “The main character is a veterinarian.”
Yelena took it gently from him. “Yes.”
“Does she ever do any veterinary work, or is this entirely about choosing between two identical men?”
“She gets to treat a dog. Briefly,” Yelena replied.
“Is that why you bought it?”
Yelena looked over the railing at the cat. “I didn't buy it. Somebody left it here. And the dog scene is the only accurate part.”

Andrew waited, but she didn't explain. He knew Yelena could help set a splint and find a fever before most of them realized someone was ill. She claimed it was because the platoon was full of idiots who hurt themselves, but she had a habit of lingering near anything injured.
“You could do that after the war,” Andrew said.
Yelena gave him a sideways look. “What, read disappointing novels professionally?”
“Work with animals.”
“I'll have a very exclusive practice,” she replied. “One cat, probably. Terrible customer.”
Andrew smiled and turned back to the road.

A flatbed truck was approaching the outpost from the east. The driver slowed to wave, and Andrew recognized a woman who regularly traded produce and spare cloth for whatever useful repairs the mechanics could manage. There had been a time when she would have sent them a bill. Now she wanted working batteries, patched tires, or somebody willing to fix a broken heater.
He waved back.

The vehicle continued toward the settlements. People were still moving materials, repairing roofs, and growing food in places that had been damaged a dozen times. The defensive line existed to give them room for those ordinary things.
Yelena nodded toward the road. “The last convoy waited hours without a working radio. If the relay goes out tomorrow, the next one waits too.”
“We're escorting the repair team tomorrow morning,” Andrew said. “Mara's found us a way around the flooded crossing.”
“Good. The cat approves.” Yelena picked up a folded note from the watch log. “Here. I measured the waterline again after breakfast.”
She had written down the levels at the eastern drainage channel. The water was climbing faster than Mara's earlier report suggested.
Andrew radioed Mara with the new readings. She acknowledged the update and confirmed the service road was still their best approach.
“Did you sleep?” she asked without looking at him.
“Of course.”
“Enough?”
Andrew considered giving her a joke. She had asked him the same question twice that week.
“Not quite,” he admitted.
“Try it tonight. It's supposed to be a remarkable experience.”
“Are you giving medical advice?”
“Just advice from someone who doesn't want her commander falling asleep while driving,” Yelena replied.
Andrew looked at the tea mug in her hand. “You could have said you were worried.”
“I could,” Yelena said.

He left her at the railing, checking her written water readings against the road. As he descended the stairs, the gray cat finally ventured out from beneath the overhang. Yelena pretended not to watch it cross toward the dish.
Darius's garden stood against the kitchen wall.

He'd built the beds from old transport crates and covered them with clear panels scavenged from storage. The plants were small and uneven but plainly alive. Andrew paused on his way to the hangar and found Darius kneeling beside a row of herbs.
“Inspection?” Darius asked without looking up.
“Just checking whether we're going to have a salad sometime this decade.”
“Not if you keep calling my plants that.”
“Sorry. I didn't know they were sensitive.”
Darius touched a leaf. “They'd be doing better if the nights were warmer.”
“Same.”
Darius rose, brushing soil from his palms. There was a little pride in the way he surveyed the beds, as if they'd accomplished something extraordinary.
“What are you making tonight?” Andrew asked.
“Stew. I've got potatoes, beans, onions, and a little cabbage left. I might use the herbs if I can spare some.”
“Can I help?”
“You can keep Nico from tasting everything before it goes into the pot.”
“That's a full-time assignment.”

Darius smiled, then grew more thoughtful. “Actually, can you make sure everyone's back before I start? Yelena's had two watch shifts today, and Sera sometimes forgets meals when she gets into a puzzle.”
Andrew nodded. “I'll round them up.”
Darius reached for his watering can. “And tell Juno to stay out of my kitchen.”
“What did he take this time?”
“Nothing today. I'm trying to preserve our winning streak.”
The first machine test began shortly after two.

Juno brought his XR-17 out of the hangar at walking speed. The six legs moved in a careful rhythm, their broad feet placing each step across the marked concrete yard. The reactor hummed through its rear housing. The cannon and missile pods were secured for the movement checks; no weapons would be fired until they reached the designated range.

Andrew and Mara stood behind the yard's safety line. Sera watched a diagnostic tablet receiving readings from the machine, while Nico held the inspection clipboard with his hearing protection hanging around his neck. He had drawn musical notes beside one of the headings until Mara reminded him that military paperwork didn't need a soundtrack.
Juno's voice came over the radio. “Left-front leg responding. Temperature normal. Ready to turn.”
Mara directed him through a slow right arc, then a left. The repaired foot lifted and settled smoothly on the wet concrete; yesterday it had caught at that same point.
“Stable temperature and load,” Sera reported. “And the new vibration pickup's clean.”
Nico made a small triumphant noise as he checked the clipboard. Sera didn't look up. “Wait for the loaded turn.”
Juno repeated the maneuver under the agreed test load. Halfway around, the machine stopped short of the last marker.
“Juno, why'd you stop?” Mara asked over the radio.
“Vibration on the left rear,” Juno answered. “Different from the bearing. Feels like a panel, but I don't want to guess.”
Sera enlarged the graph. “I'm seeing it. The repaired joint is steady. Something farther back is rattling when the weight shifts.”

Andrew looked from the tablet to the machine. The gun test was still ahead of them. He could have told Juno to continue and save time, but that was exactly the kind of decision he was trying to stop making.
“Bring her back to the service apron,” Andrew said into the radio. “We'll find it before we fire anything.”

Juno returned at a crawl. With the machine shut down and secured, he and Nico found a loose exterior bracket near the left rear armor. It was a small fault, nothing to do with the repaired bearing, but Andrew was glad Juno had reported it. A heavy cannon shot was not the moment to discover what else could shake loose.
Juno secured the bracket, and Sera checked the sensor reading again. The second movement check was clean.

The live-fire lane lay beyond the rear earthworks, with an observation shelter tucked behind a concrete wall. Rain had darkened the target posts and left the service track muddy. At the far end of the lane, a reinforced practice target waited in front of a high dirt backstop.

They had authorization for one full-power cannon discharge. The test needed to prove the leg could withstand recoil; putting more heat and strain through the weapon than necessary would be a waste, even if the range had the power to spare.

Nobody in the shelter needed a lesson in how an XR-17 fired. Every one of them had trained in the cockpit, and each knew the peculiar way the whole machine seemed to brace itself just before the main cannon went off. Today they were watching the left-front leg, not learning to shoot.

Juno brought his XR-17 onto the mark and settled it on all six feet. The machine crouched lower as the legs took the load. Above the cockpit, the turret turned toward the target. The upright missile pods remained still on either side of the cannon.

Andrew stood beside Mara in the observation shelter. Sera had her diagnostic tablet propped against the window ledge. Nico stood behind them, peering around Andrew's shoulder even though there was plenty of room to his left.
“Juno, how's she feeling?” Mara asked over the radio.
“Beautiful. Absolutely beautiful.”
“The cannon or your repair?” Nico asked.
“Yes.”
Andrew laughed. “Remember what we're here for.”
“To witness my genius under controlled conditions?”
“To find out whether your front leg stays attached,” Sera replied.
“It'll stay attached,” Juno said. “I checked it twice.”
“And we all know you'd never make a mistake,” Mara said.
“Finally, some recognition.”
Sera glanced at her screen. “Recorder's running. The left-front channel looks good.”

Beyond the glass, the XR-17's reactor housing brightened. A low vibration rolled across the ground as the cannon charged. Heat stirred the air around the barrel, and thin lines of white-gold light came alive along the assembly.
Nico leaned forward. He'd fired the same weapon in training, but Andrew knew that look. Watching someone else's cannon charge never got old.
Mara lifted her radio. “Okay, Juno. Weapons free. Fire when rea—”
The cannon discharged.
A column of white-hot energy tore downrange. The shelter shook as the report hit them, hard enough that Andrew felt it through the soles of his boots. Dust leapt from the firing lane.

The target vanished inside the impact. The beam carried through to the hillside beyond, carving a brilliant wound in the dirt backstop. For an instant the earth glowed orange-white; then it slumped inward, its surface glassy where the heat had fused the soil.
The XR-17 rocked backward. Its six legs dug in, absorbed the force, and brought the hull level again. Andrew watched the repaired left-front joint compress and recover without the slightest hitch.
“...dy,” Mara finished into the radio.
Nobody spoke for a beat. Then Nico burst out laughing.
“Did he just—” Nico started.
“He did,” Sera said, her eyes still on the readings.
Mara lowered the radio and looked at Andrew. “I hadn't even finished the word.”
Andrew tried to keep his face straight. He failed.
“Juno,” Mara said.
“Yeah?”
“I was still talking.”
“You said weapons free!”
“I also said fire when ready.”
“I was ready.”
“Clearly,” Mara said.
Across the range, steam rose from the crater. Nico was still laughing. Andrew watched the XR-17 standing steady on the mark, its cannon cooling above the cockpit, and shook his head.
Sera enlarged the recoil trace. “Hang on. The leg took the whole load. No binding, no abnormal vibration. Look at that recovery.”
Juno went quiet. “Wait. Seriously?”
“Seriously. It's clean.”
“HA! I KNEW IT!”
His shout crackled so loudly through the speaker that Nico pulled his headset away from one ear.
“You're more excited about the bearing than the target,” Andrew said.
“I fixed the bearing,” Juno replied. “The cannon was going to do that anyway.”
Mara studied the crater for a moment, then keyed the radio again. “Bring her back in, Juno. Walking speed. Let's have a look at that leg.”
“Copy. Can I shoot again?”
“That was our only authorized discharge,” Sera said.
“So that's a no?”
“That's a no,” Andrew and Mara answered together.
Juno sighed with theatrical disappointment, then turned the XR-17 toward the depot. Nico began imitating the cannon's noise until Mara told him his version needed less spit.

Back in the hangar, Juno went straight to the repaired leg. Nico checked the alignment marks beneath the armor while Sera compared the recoil trace to the earlier load test. Mara stood ready with the inspection sheet.
“No shift,” Nico called. “Still lined up.”
“The joint stayed within limits all the way through recoil,” Sera said. “No hidden vibration, either.”
Mara signed the clearance and handed it to Andrew. “Fit for tomorrow.”
Andrew gave the sheet to Juno. “Good work.” Juno glanced at the leg, his usual grin settling into something smaller and genuinely pleased.
Outside, the rain had started again. Juno glanced toward the yard and the empty camera tripod. “I was hoping she'd get a photograph while the mech was clean.”
“Akari's working on it,” Andrew said.
As if she'd heard her name, Akari appeared in the doorway. “Four o'clock. Nobody disappears.”
Mara looked past her at the wet concrete. “It's raining.”
“I have a plan,” Akari said.
Andrew looked at her determined face. He doubted the weather would get the last word.
At four seventeen, Akari declared the weather officially cooperative.

The rain had stopped, although water still dripped from the gutters. She set the tripod on a dry patch of concrete and inspected the viewfinder with an expression usually reserved for people checking a weapon sight.
Mara came out of the hangar first, carrying her folded route sheet.
“Is this going to take long?” she asked Akari.
“That depends entirely on whether you cooperate,” Akari replied.
“Then yes,” Mara said.
Akari ignored her and adjusted the camera again.

Andrew had spent the last ten minutes collecting people. Yelena had wanted to finish the watch log before leaving her post. Darius had insisted on checking the rising dough for tonight's bread. Nico had disappeared to find a jacket he considered presentable, which turned out to be one with a large rip at the elbow.
Sera was already by the tripod, helping Akari keep the lens clean.
“You forgot your spare battery,” Sera told her.
“I was going to get it,” Akari replied.
“You said that about the last three things I brought you.”
“That's because you're exceptionally useful.”
Sera placed the battery into Akari's hand. “I'm charging for my services.”
“Will you accept friendship?” Akari asked.
“I'll consider it,” Sera said.

Andrew watched Sera make a tiny adjustment to the camera's angle while Akari checked the image. The two of them could argue for twenty minutes over a photograph and somehow understand each other perfectly.

Juno emerged from the hangar with his goggles pushed into his bright hair. He'd spent most of the walk back from the range praising the recoil trace and telling anyone who would listen exactly why the new bearing had held. He glanced up at the turret, still looking entirely too pleased with himself.
“Go on,” Akari said. “What?”
“I was going to ask if we could turn the cannon toward the camera,” Juno admitted.
Mara folded her arms. “Not today.”
“I know,” Juno said. He didn't argue.
Andrew was relieved. He had spent enough of the afternoon listening to Juno talk about that cannon.
Akari waved him toward the group. “Good. Then use that energy to stand still for ten seconds.”
Juno looked at the battered XR-17. “Can I at least stand on the good side?”
“It has a good side?” Sera asked.
Juno gave her a pained look, then grinned despite himself.

The eight of them gathered beneath the broad front of the center machine. Its six legs framed the group, the angular cockpit hanging above them. Against the enormous feet and heavy armored body, even Darius looked smaller than usual.
“Closer together,” Akari called from the tripod.
Nico shuffled sideways and bumped Darius's shoulder.
“Closer,” Akari repeated.
Nico pressed against Darius so firmly that Darius nearly lost his balance.
“Not inside him,” Akari said.
“Instructions unclear,” Nico answered.
Yelena took Nico by the back of his jacket and pulled him into a less dangerous position.
“Stand here,” she said. “And stop bouncing.”
“I've got a song stuck in my head,” Nico explained.
“Then keep it there,” Yelena told him.
Mara moved beside Andrew. Her uniform trousers were still marked by the mud from the morning inspection.
“If this picture ends up on an official noticeboard,” she said, “I want it known that I objected.”
“Your objection is noted,” Andrew replied. “On an unofficial basis.”
Akari waved from the camera. “Are you two finished?”
“Never,” Mara said.
“Good. Look at me,” Akari called.
Sera crouched, checked the camera's focus one last time, then stood and joined the others. Akari set the timer for ten seconds and ran toward the group.
At six seconds, she saw the camera strap dangling across the corner of the lens.
“Wait,” Akari called.
She doubled back, fixed the strap, and tried again. At three seconds Nico stepped onto Mara's boot. Mara reached for his arm, but Nico tipped toward Juno, who caught him by the collar.
Andrew started laughing.
Akari made it into place just as the camera clicked.
For a moment she stood there breathing hard, then hurried back to the tripod.
“Well?” Darius asked.
Akari inspected the screen. “Oh.”

The others gathered around her, passing the camera carefully from hand to hand. The picture was a disaster by any official standard. Nico's eyes were wide with alarm, Mara was holding Juno's sleeve, and Andrew had his head turned toward the commotion. Akari was still moving into position, her ponytail caught halfway through a swing.
Darius had somehow managed to smile normally.
“This one's going on the wall,” he said.
Mara made a noise of disbelief. “Absolutely not.”
Akari pulled the camera back to her chest. “Absolutely yes.”
“Can you at least take another where I have both feet on the ground?” Mara asked.
“I can,” Akari said. “But I like this one better.”
Sera looked at the screen again. Her expression softened. “Me too.”
Andrew studied the photograph. No one looked disciplined or heroic. They looked like themselves on an ordinary afternoon, still arguing over where to stand.
“Print it when you can,” he told Akari. “Darius will find a place for it.”
“I already know where,” Darius said.
Akari beamed. “Finally, someone understands art.”
By half past four the courtyard was empty again. Andrew went back to the hangar long enough to file the signed machine clearance. The photograph had somehow taken more arguing than the entire test.
Juno was still at the workbench, turning the worn bearing ring in his hands.
Its outer ring had enough sound metal to make a spacer for a workshop fixture, and he disliked throwing away anything he could reuse. Dried grease clung stubbornly to the groove.
“For the mech?” Andrew asked.
“No. A cleaning fixture. I need the ring washed before I can fit it. The workshop soak tray's already full.”
“Use the proper gear and keep it away from flight parts,” Andrew said.
Juno nodded and returned to the bench. Andrew left him there and headed for his office.
The trouble began before five.
Andrew had returned to his office to check the next morning's briefing when Darius called from the kitchen.
“Andrew. Come here.”
It wasn't the voice Darius had used at breakfast. Andrew put down his pencil.

In the kitchen, Darius stood beside the worktable with his large steel stew pot in both hands. This was the pot he normally used when there were eight hungry people waiting for dinner. It was wide, deep, and nearly impossible to replace. The military stores had no spare, and the civilian market wouldn't hand one over for a few ration slips.
Inside lay the old bearing. Brown cleaning liquid surrounded it. Grease marked the rim.
Juno stood near the doorway, his newly washed hands still damp. Nico was beside him, holding the lid and looking like he wanted to be somewhere else.
Andrew stared into the pot.
“What happened?” he asked.

Juno spoke first. “I told Nico to find a spare soaking basin. When he brought this into the workshop, I assumed it was one of ours. I was watching the bearing, not the container, and I poured the degreaser before I checked.”
Nico tightened his grip on the lid. “The workshop tray was full. I knew Darius kept a big pot, and I thought we could scrub it afterward.”
Darius set the pot down carefully. “You took the thing I cook for all of us in and filled it with degreaser?”
Nico looked at the table. “When you put it like that…”
“How else should I put it?” Darius asked.
Juno stepped forward. “I told him to fetch a basin, and I didn't check what he brought. I should have. This is on me too.”
“It's had degreaser and machine grease in it,” Darius said. “We don't use that for food again. That's not a matter of scrubbing harder.”
Juno looked down at the pot, then at the ingredients Darius had arranged across the table. Potatoes, onions, cabbage, beans. Everything was ready, except the thing meant to hold it.
“I didn't think about where it had come from,” Juno said, more quietly. “Or what you needed it for tonight.”
Darius took a moment before answering. “That's the problem.”
Andrew didn't hurry to fill the silence. Darius had every right to be angry; Juno and Nico had made a choice that could have harmed someone. A joke wouldn't fix it.
“Juno,” Andrew said, “take the pot out of the kitchen. Label it for workshop use only.”
Juno nodded.
“Nico, help him,” Andrew said. “Then both of you check stores for a replacement. Don't bring back something that might have been used for chemicals.”
“I understand,” Nico said.
Juno lifted the pot by both handles, keeping it clear of the food. “Darius, I'm sorry. I should have asked, and I should have known better.”
Darius looked at him. “I know you weren't trying to ruin dinner.”
“I'll replace it,” Juno promised.
“I'd appreciate that,” Darius answered.
Juno carried the pot into the hall with Nico following. For once, neither had anything clever to say.
Andrew stayed with Darius. The cook stood looking at the vegetables he'd prepared, his hands resting on the edge of the table.
“You planned this all day,” Andrew said.
Darius let out a slow breath. “I had. I wanted something everyone could sit down to and enjoy.”
“They still can,” Andrew said. “Maybe not the same thing.”
Darius surveyed the two frying pans hanging above the stove and a small saucepan on the shelf. After a while he reached for the first pan.
“We'll make fried potatoes and cabbage,” Darius said. “Beans on the side. The bread's nearly ready.”
“That sounds good,” Andrew replied.
“It wasn't the plan,” Darius said.
“No,” Andrew agreed. “What do you need from me?”
Darius pushed a bowl of cabbage toward him. “Wash your hands. Then tear that into pieces. I'll tell you if they're wrong.”
Andrew rolled up his sleeves and went to the sink.
The day had taken a turn he hadn't planned for either. For once, he wasn't going to make it worse by trying to control every detail.
The kitchen became crowded within minutes.

Nico returned from the stores with clean hands and no replacement pot. He had found a small saucepan, but it was already on the kitchen shelf and was only big enough for the beans. Darius had him wash the vegetables instead.
Juno came back a little later carrying the inventory book.
“There's nothing food-safe in workshop stores,” Juno told Darius. “I checked every shelf, and I'm not bringing you something with an unknown history.”
“Good,” Darius said without turning from the stove.

“I put in a request for a proper replacement,” Juno continued. “If stores can't find one, I'll take some of my own repaired tools to the civilian market and see who'll trade. A proper pot, food-safe. I promise.”
Darius stirred the onions. “I'd appreciate it.”
The response wasn't warm, but Juno seemed to understand that it was more than he'd earned so far.
“Can I do anything now?” Juno asked.
Darius pointed at the sink. “Wash the mixing bowls. With dish soap. Not anything you found in the hangar.”
“Fair,” Juno answered.

Andrew tore cabbage leaves into pieces while Darius moved potatoes around the hot pan. The vegetables hissed when they touched the oil. By now the smell was so good that Andrew could hear Nico's stomach making its opinion known from the other side of the table.
Nico held up a potato slice thick enough to stand on its edge. Darius studied it, then showed him how to steady the potato and turn his knife.
Nico tried again. The second slice was thinner, though still not particularly even.
“Better,” Darius said.
“I'm a natural,” Nico replied, but he was watching Darius's hands closely.

On the wall above the stove was a chalkboard where Darius wrote the evening meal. Earlier he'd written STEW. He studied it for a second, then erased the word and replaced it with POTATOES, CABBAGE, BEANS, BREAD.
Nico inspected the revised chalkboard menu, then glanced at the heap of potatoes. He tapped the handle of his knife against the table, trying out a rhythm.
“Not with my knives,” Darius said.
“It's a good beat,” Nico protested.
“It's a knife,” Darius said, and went back to his onions.
Andrew moved the knife away from Nico's tapping fingers. “Use the table instead.”
Nico drummed on the table for another few seconds, then stopped when he noticed Andrew watching.
“What?” Nico asked.
“Nothing. I didn't know you could do that,” Andrew answered.
“It's just a rhythm,” Nico said.
“You made it up?”
“Mostly,” Nico said. “I've been trying to put a song together. There's nowhere quiet to work on it.”
Andrew considered the packed building, the mechanical noise, the arguments over the radio, and the kitchen that was currently occupied by half the squad.
“Fair criticism,” he admitted. “You could use the common room after the movie.”
Nico hesitated. “Maybe.”
Darius looked over his shoulder. “I'd listen.”
“It's not finished,” Nico said quickly.
“Neither was breakfast when you complained about it,” Darius answered. “I fed you anyway.”
Nico reddened and went back to his potatoes. Andrew let him. For someone who was forever demanding attention, Nico didn't seem to know what to do when it came for something he'd made.
Akari entered carrying the camera, which she placed safely on a shelf out of reach of the food.
“Please tell me I smell dinner,” she said.
“You smell the frying pan,” Darius replied.
“Wonderful. Can I taste something?” Akari asked.
“When it's ready,” Darius said.
Akari took in the chopped vegetables, Juno at the sink, and Nico holding a strangely large potato slice. Her gaze went to the empty space where the big pot normally stood.
“I heard what happened,” she said.
Juno looked down at the bowl in his hands. “Yeah.”
Akari paused. “That was a pretty stupid thing to do.”
“It was,” Juno said.
She seemed satisfied with the answer. “Do you need me to ask around about another pot? The driver I traded with for my camera strap sometimes brings kitchen supplies. She might know somebody.”
Darius looked at her with interest. “Could you?”
“I'll write it down,” Akari said. “But don't count on anything until I hear back.”
“Thank you,” Darius said.
Akari smiled and reached toward a crisp potato at the edge of the pan.
Darius caught her hand before she could take it. “That one stays.”
“You have excellent reflexes,” she observed.
“I've been cooking for you all.”
Sera arrived just behind Akari, holding the projector remote and a small folded piece of cardboard. She stayed in the doorway, away from the busy stove.
“The projector works,” Sera announced.
Juno turned from the sink. “Did you repair the mount?”
“I improved the picture,” Sera answered.
“That's not the same thing,” Juno said.
“It's the thing we needed,” Sera replied.
Sera held up the folded cardboard, pleased with herself for once. Akari grinned at her.
“Does this mean I get to choose a movie?” Akari asked.
“You chose the last one,” Sera said. “The bird documentary.”
“Everybody liked the birds,” Akari said.
“Nico slept through them.”
“Not the eagle,” Nico called from the table.
Sera looked at Andrew. “Can I pick tonight?”
Andrew blinked. Sera usually allowed the others to argue themselves into a decision, then read a book through whatever film they eventually chose.
“Sure,” he said. “What do you want to watch?”
“Something funny,” Sera replied. “And I don't want anyone explaining the ending before it happens.”
Nico made a wounded noise.
“We can negotiate the second condition,” he suggested.
“We can't,” Sera said.
Mara appeared in the doorway holding the patrol folder. “Tomorrow's route and Juno's clearance are signed. Your copy's on the desk, Andrew.”
Andrew nodded. “Thanks. I'll brief everyone in the morning.”
Darius lifted a wooden spoon toward the folder. “Then it can stay out of my kitchen.”
Mara tucked the papers under her arm. “Understood.”
By the time they carried dinner into the common room, the building smelled of browned potatoes, warm bread, pepper, and onions.

The room had been designed for a different set of occupants. Its chairs were the kind that could be wiped clean in seconds, and the tables looked as if they'd once held municipal paperwork. The squad had added cushions, drawings, a bookshelf made from packing crates, and a temperamental projector aimed at an empty patch of wall. A board-game score sheet hung beside the duty schedule, complete with an argument about whether Nico's latest victory counted.

Andrew brought in eight cups. He set them at the places around the table and counted without meaning to. Eight people would eat together tonight. He could hear them arriving down the corridor, each voice recognizable before its owner appeared.
Darius came in with the pans and set them on the table.
“It isn't the stew I planned,” he told everyone. “But it should be good.”
Andrew took a piece of potato, tasted it, and went back for another.
Darius watched him. “Well?”
“Very good,” Andrew said.
“You mean it?”
“I wouldn't risk a second piece otherwise.”
Darius laughed, finally sitting down to eat with the others.
Across the table, Mara lifted one of Nico's thick potato slices.
“Did you cut this?” she asked.
Nico considered it. “Possibly.”
“It's bigger than the bread,” Mara said.
“I didn't know there was a limit,” Nico answered.
“There's a practical limit,” Darius told him. “And then there's what you've made.”
Nico stuck his fork into the potato and managed to smile. “I'll improve.”
“You did improve,” Darius said. “The later ones are much better.”
The small compliment shut Nico up more effectively than any threat Mara had made all day.

They ate for a while without anybody trying to perform. The room was warm, and the fried onions tasted good with the beans. Akari asked whether Darius had saved enough bread for breakfast. Yelena wanted to know whether the garden had produced anything useful. Sera listened to Nico explain his unfinished song, asking him one question that made him stop and think.

Andrew looked around the table. All eight of them had different tasks tomorrow, different concerns, and different ideas of what counted as entertainment. Tonight the biggest argument was over whose turn it was to wash the pans.
Darius raised a piece of bread toward Juno.
“You did the bowls,” he said. “You can leave the pans to me.”
Juno looked surprised. “Are you sure?”
“Yes. But don't borrow them.”
Juno held up both hands. “I won't.”
Yelena put her empty plate aside and brought out a battered deck of cards.
“Darius,” she said, “you still owe me a rematch.”
Darius smiled. “You still owe me two biscuits.”
“That's a separate financial matter,” Yelena replied.
“You ate them,” he replied.
“And you should have guarded them better.”
Andrew watched Darius reach for the cards. The day had not gone as any of them intended. Dinner was good anyway.
Yelena won the first hand by two points. Darius accused her of neglecting to explain a rule about matching cards.
“I explained it,” she said, already dealing again.
“You explained most of it,” Darius muttered. Yelena ignored him, which was how he knew she'd heard.
The projector came on, its picture leaning slightly to the left. Sera watched it for a second, folded a square of cardboard, and pushed it beneath the rear foot. The image straightened on the wall.
“Fixed,” she said.
Juno looked over from his headphones. “That mount really needs replacing.”
“The film's ninety minutes,” Sera said. “The cardboard only has to last that long.”
Juno considered the argument, then went back to his seat.

Andrew leaned against the arm of the couch while they settled in. Mara occupied a chair with her boots tucked beneath it. Nico took the seat closest to the projector, insisting that it had the best sound, though he'd spent most of the afternoon complaining about the film choice.
Sera put on the comedy she'd selected. Nobody challenged her a second time.
For the opening ten minutes, Nico tried to explain how he would handle every situation differently. Sera gave him a look. Nico held up his hands and, with impressive effort, stopped talking.

Andrew laughed at a scene in which a man tried to smuggle food out of a banquet under his coat. It was the sort of ridiculous problem the actors treated with such seriousness that he couldn't help enjoying it.
He stayed through the next scene, too.
Then he checked the wall clock.

There were still a few minutes of work he'd promised himself. Tomorrow's route was settled, and Juno's machine had passed the final inspection, but Andrew wanted to review the handover notes and make sure the technicians would have a clear place to wait while the squad secured the road.
He slipped off the arm of the couch.
Akari noticed. “Where are you going?”
“Office,” Andrew said. “I'll be back.”
She looked at the clock. “You said that after dinner yesterday.”
“I came back,” Andrew said.
“After the credits,” she replied.
Andrew couldn't argue with that. “I'll try to beat my record.”
Akari turned toward the film, not quite satisfied, but she didn't ask him to stay.
The corridor was cooler than the common room. He passed the kitchen, where the pans were drying on a rack, and reached his small office beside the hangar.

The room was barely wide enough for a desk, two chairs, and a filing cabinet. The desk lamp cast a warm circle over the maps. A spare set of gloves hung from a nail beside the door. Andrew had promised to put up a proper coat hook, but there were always things with higher priority.

Mara's revised route was clear on the map. The flooded bridge was marked off, the alternate road checked, and the escort's waiting point agreed. He had already seen the signatures. He opened the notebook anyway.
Andrew wrote the single handover note the technicians would need, then set the pen down. The rest of tomorrow could wait until tomorrow. He sat another moment, as if expecting the work to object.
An old photograph was pinned beside the desk lamp.

Twelve people stood crowded between two XR-17s, several of them laughing before the camera had even been set. The picture had been taken when the whole original unit was together. Their uniforms looked newer, and Matthias Adler stood at the back with two fingers hooked into Andrew's collar.
Andrew remembered Matthias doing it just as Akari called for everybody to stand still. He'd been laughing and trying to pull away when the camera clicked.

Matthias had been twenty-one, and somehow capable of making every terrible joke sound like an official order. He'd claimed the photograph proved that Andrew was too impatient to stand still for ten seconds.
Andrew touched the edge of the paper.

Four people in the old picture no longer came to breakfast. Sometimes an everyday thing reminded him of one of them: an argument over a game, an empty place by the repair bench, a song somebody used to complain about and now played without thinking.
He didn't stand there trying to find a lesson in the photograph. He knew their faces well enough.

Earlier that afternoon Akari had taken another picture, this time of the eight who were still together. He remembered Mara holding Juno's sleeve, Nico nearly falling, and Akari barely making it into the frame.
He found himself smiling.
A knock interrupted him.
Darius stood in the doorway holding a little plate and a jar.
“Are you hiding?” Darius asked.
“Working,” Andrew replied.
“Can you do both?” Darius asked.
“Apparently,” Andrew answered.

Darius came in and put the plate on a clear corner of the desk. A small roll sat on it, split and toasted. He unscrewed the jar and spread a thin layer of jam across the bread, taking care to reach the edges.
Andrew read the label.
“Strawberry?” he asked. “Where did you get that?”
“I know people,” Darius said.
“What sort of people?”
“People who appreciate bread.”
Andrew took a bite. The toast cracked beneath his teeth, and the sweet taste made him stop thinking about the map long enough to notice how hungry he still was.
“That's really good,” he said.
“It's jam and bread.”
“Don't undersell yourself.”
Darius leaned against the filing cabinet and looked at the completed route sheet.
“How was the inspection?” he asked.
“Passed,” Andrew said. “All of it. Juno's machine is cleared.”
“Good.” Darius hesitated. “He came by afterward. Said he'd start looking for a proper pot first thing tomorrow.”
“I know.”
“I don't want him thinking I'm angry forever.”
“He knows you're not,” Andrew said. “But he should know you're angry tonight.”
Darius considered that. “I am.”
“Then you can still be angry and make him breakfast.”
“That might be generous.”
“You're very generous.”
Darius shook his head, smiling.

From the common room came a burst of laughter, then a familiar voice protesting that the film's main character was making a terrible decision. Nico's voice. It had a distinctive way of climbing whenever he felt that an imaginary person ought to listen to his advice.
Darius glanced toward the door. “You're missing it.”
“I'm almost finished,” Andrew said.
“How much is almost?”
He glanced at the map. “Five minutes.”
Darius looked at him.
“I know,” Andrew said. “You've heard that before.”
“I have.”

Andrew sat for another moment. The route was confirmed. Tomorrow's assignment would be explained at the morning briefing. Mara and the others had done their work, and he'd checked it. There was nothing on the table that needed another hour tonight.
He put down the pen.
“Come on,” he said. “Before Nico starts directing the film himself.”
Darius stepped aside and let him pass.

The common room had grown warm and crowded. Akari had claimed the couch beside Sera, who was watching the film with the pleased concentration of someone whose choice had finally been accepted. Yelena and Mara were following the story from the chairs, occasionally exchanging a comment. Nico sat on the floor with a cushion behind his back, still whispering occasional advice to the actors.
Juno looked up when Andrew came in.
“Did you finish the briefing?” Juno asked.
“Finished,” Andrew said. “You can stop worrying about it.”
“I wasn't,” Juno said.
“You asked,” Andrew replied.
“I was being supportive,” Juno insisted.
Andrew sat down in the space beside Akari. She lifted her feet to let him through, then put them across his knees as soon as he settled.
“I charge for this,” he told her.
“Put it on my account,” Akari said without looking away from the screen.

Darius returned to his card game with Yelena, who had somehow talked him into playing a third round. Andrew balanced his plate on one hand, trying to decide whether the film's leading man was supposed to be clever or simply lucky.
Akari reached for his toast.
He caught her wrist gently.
“Ask Darius,” Andrew whispered.
“I did,” she whispered back. “He said you'd share.”
Across the room Darius looked up, met Andrew's eyes, and gave him an unapologetic shrug.
Andrew broke the toast in half.
Akari accepted her share with a satisfied smile. On the wall the hero finally escaped through the window, only to discover that he'd climbed into the wrong garden.
Nico groaned. Sera laughed. Even Mara covered her mouth.
Andrew stayed until the credits.
